paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1987, the economist Robert Solow quipped that you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. At the time, businesses had invested heavily in computers for over a decade, yet measured output per worker had grown only slowly. The puzzle, known as the productivity paradox, has returned in recent years with artificial intelligence, digital platforms and cloud computing: technologies that seem transformative yet appear to have done little to accelerate growth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Several explanations have been proposed. The first is mismeasurement. Official statistics are good at counting cars and washing machines but poor at capturing improvements in quality or the value of free services. A smartphone contains a camera, map, music player and encyclopaedia that once cost thousands of pounds, yet in the statistics, it counts as a single product. Economists disagree about the size of the gap; some estimates suggest it accounts for a minor part of the slowdown, others for a larger part.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second explanation is delay. Historically, general-purpose technologies take decades to transform the economy. Electricity was introduced to factories in the 1880s, but productivity did not rise until the 1920s, because manufacturers at first merely replaced steam engines with electric motors, leaving the layout of the factory unchanged. Real gains came only when they redesigned production around the new flexibility, placing machines wherever the work required. The economist Paul David argued that computers may follow the same pattern: organisations take time to rethink how they work.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third explanation is that the ideas themselves have become harder to find. Some researchers argue that each new increment of progress demands more researchers and more money than before. If so, the slowdown reflects a genuine decline in the returns to innovation rather than a statistical illusion. A fourth view, favoured by sceptics, is that recent digital innovations simply matter less for productivity than the great inventions of the past, such as sanitation, the combustion engine and antibiotics.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These accounts are not mutually exclusive, and the truth probably involves elements of each. What the debate shows is how difficult it is to assess technology's impact while we are living through it. The electricity example is a cautionary tale for both optimists and pessimists: those who expected immediate transformation were disappointed, but those who concluded that nothing had changed were also wrong.
